directions.litai: Speak in clear natural American English, as an experienced female engineer making a persuasive live demonstration to a skeptical colleague. Warm, brisk, direct, dry humor. Respond to the objection, never sound like an announcer. Do not laugh unless the words call for it.
directions.sam: Speak in natural American English, as an experienced male software engineer cross-examining a vendor's demonstration. Wry, skeptical, concise, alert. Real questions, not a narrator. Not hostile, not theatrical.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: I'm Sam. C++, make, tests. They work. You've got ten minutes to convince me I need another tool. The clock includes buzzwords.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: I'm Litai, from Literate AI. Keep your tools; I'm selling a harness, not a religion. The interesting part is between an agent saying done and a product being ready.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: My tests already tell me that. Are we adding YAML so a chatbot can feel supervised?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: If your pipeline already proves every step, keep it. The gap is when an agent implements the wrong promise, tests that same misunderstanding, and calls the package shipped. Let's inspect one promise before generating anything.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: You get one small example. Not a cathedral of configuration.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: One promise. A greeting card: a name and messages in; a greeting, a recipient identifier and counts out. That promise is the Component, Unicode whitespace included. It says nothing about how it's built.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So, a requirements file. We've had those since before the coffee machine had firmware.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Yes, except this one is bound to the work. Flavors are the build choices: language, build system, platform, packaging. Swap a Flavor and you still need a real toolchain and new tests. No magic porting. The promise stays put.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And your recorded example is Python. You brought Python to a C++ interview.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Guilty. The smallest recorded run is Python plus Make. Your kind of code shows up in a few minutes: C++, CMake, CTest.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Then stop drawing and run something. Starting with where I get it.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Repository and commands are on screen. On macOS: Python three eleven or newer, Git and Make, then make install. This panel is a walkthrough. The terminal sessions are a recorded development build, revisions beside the film.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: A development build. So, tomorrow's features on loan.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Possibly, which is why it's labeled. This is its real read-only create plan, pinned to a public parent commit. Destination and choices are reviewable; nothing applies until you acknowledge it.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Fine. Where's the actual agent writing code?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Here. Rebuild invokes the selected coding agent, with explicit permission to run generated code in this disposable project. Edited replay; the waiting is compressed.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: A greeting card doesn't prove it can maintain my parser.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: It doesn't. It makes the mechanism inspectable before we touch your parser. This generated code normalizes the recipient and counts words.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: These generated tests are useful, but they're not our independent definition of correct.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: There. Red. Missing messages. Your ten-minute sales pitch appears to have developed a warranty claim.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Fair. The Component requires messages; the inherited acceptance case got that wrong. That's a defect in our starter, not the agent's. That recorded defect is tracked for an upstream fix.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Hold on. Your independent check, the thing meant to catch the agent, was the broken part. And then you edited it until it went green.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Then judge my edit against the written contract, not the generated code: two messages, six words, this identifier. We corrected this disposable project's acceptance cases and reran. Local recovery, disclosed. That recorded parent still needs repair.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And if it had been wrong the other way, too lenient, you'd be green and smiling.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Yes. A lenient oracle passes bad code, and so does a wrong specification; the harness can't detect either on its own. It puts the contract, the acceptance cases and the results where a reviewer can challenge them. Recorded results, skips included.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Green on your machine. My release checklist is longer than that.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Agreed. Local wheel and package verification; no registry upload. Publishing is a separate decision. Tests of one revision don't qualify another, and a green build doesn't prove the installed package works.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: My real project already has years of C++. I'm not replacing that with an optimistic paragraph.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Don't. Here is TinyXML2, pinned to the recorded public commit. The adoption plan inspects the existing project before mutation. We preserve the original implementation, establish a recovery point, and wrap its real build and tests.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Which tests? If you replace CTest with an agent congratulating itself, we're finished.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Its own CMake targets and CTest, run on the preserved source. In rehearsal we also hit a bug in our CTest-summary parser; it was repaired and the harness run repeated.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: That's two bugs in your own tool in one demo. Why does it go anywhere near my CI?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Fair count. It shouldn't, until a trial earns it. What a trial gets you: a repeatable baseline, recorded build and test evidence, and a written account of what's authoritative. Wrapped: the harness surrounds your code. Retained: that preserved code has its required baseline evidence.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And then comes the upsell to a rewrite.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: There are later stages: draft specifications, regenerate, and qualify against independent evidence before authority moves. None of that is complete in this demo. You can stop at retained; your original source still governs releases.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Shared practice, workers, and two kinds of orchestration
turns.text: Fine. Now there's a framework-shaped pile of files beside my code, times every repository. Does my agent read that whole grab bag to fix a typo?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: No. Agent skills guide tasks like adoption or release; generation skills guide building one Component with its Flavors. Nested skills add focused guidance to their parents; a generation recipe pins its selected instructions. Shared rules come through tracked inheritance: framework, your team's conventions, then each product. This part is a diagram, not a run.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Inherited means Tuesday's upstream cleverness rewrites Monday's release.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Not silently. A recorded revision isn't a live subscription. An update plan, like this recorded one, compares what you inherited, what you changed and what's new upstream. Conflicts wait for a decision. Upgrading the tool itself is separate, and an old receipt isn't fresh proof.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And when two parents disagree?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Ambiguous definitions are rejected. A product can override deliberately, with provenance. Prefer a narrow project rule to copying a whole policy. Inheritance shares practice; it doesn't remove review.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Including this video? Every project inherits two talking heads?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: No. The video-production skill is reusable; this cast belongs to this repository. Your payment library is not contractually obliged to include a sarcastic man.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: I supply that service free. Now the bill: a cluster, a platform team, another subscription?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: One machine, as this recording used. Compatible machines you already have can become workers: addresses and credentials in private configuration, then probe toolchains and agent access. Walkthrough, not an SSH run.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And Agentis, the orchestrator? Two systems supervising one agent sounds like two managers in one meeting.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Different jobs. The orchestrator assigns work. Literate AI structures specification, generation, checks and release evidence. A prompt saying be careful isn't a gate. No deployed Agentis integration is shown here.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: My product is three repositories that depend on each other. Is that inheritance, or more orchestration?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Repository orchestration, a different one from Agentis; sorry about the word. It records child pins and dependency order. Inheritance shares practice; Agentis assigns agent work. Three graphs. Each child still needs its own evidence. Diagram, not a deployment.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: AI slop with a receipt is still AI slop.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Yes. A receipt records checks; it doesn't certify taste, usefulness or requirements. Independent acceptance is how you challenge the output. Humans need that too. We've just been better at declining supervision.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Time. I won't migrate everything. I'll try one library at retained, compare the overhead, and keep my Makefile. If it's busywork, it goes.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: That's a fair trial. Start with one useful boundary, inspect the plan, keep a baseline, and judge the result. The pitch isn't trust the agent. It's make the claims testable, including mine.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Don't look pleased. You've earned a trial, not a convert.
